answer: At the rates of the week of 2026-09-24 (30-year 7.03%, 15-year 6.42%), a $320,000 15-year loan costs $2,773.49 a month. Paying the 30-year loan off in the same 15 years takes $2,881.62 a month: $108.13 more each month and $19,464 more over 15 years. Paying only the 15-year payment on the 30-year loan finishes in 192.9 months, about a year late. The 30-year loan's required payment is $2,135.42, so that $19,464 is the price of being allowed to drop to the lower payment. Across 1,831 weeks since August 1991 the 30-year rate was 0.2 to 1.0 point above the 15-year (mean 0.57; at least half a point in 62.9% of weeks), and the same extra cost ranged from $6,097 to $29,502 (median $16,594). History, not a forecast.
guess: People who plan to prepay usually assume a 30-year paid like a 15-year is 'basically the same' as a 15-year mortgage, costing at most a few thousand dollars more.
changesDecision: The flexibility is not free: at today's spread it is about $108 a month and close to $19,500 over 15 years on $320,000, and it has never cost less than about $6,100 since 1991. A buyer can weigh that dollar figure against how much they value the right to fall back to the required 30-year payment, about $640 below the 15-year payment, instead of treating the two plans as equal.

assumptions: Loan $320,000, fixed rate, level monthly payments, no points, fees, taxes, insurance or escrow.
The weekly survey averages stand for the rates a typical borrower would be offered on each term in the same week.
Paying the 30-year loan 'on a 15-year schedule' means a level payment that retires it in exactly 180 months at the 30-year rate.
No discounting, no investment of payment differences, no tax effects.
limits: History, not a forecast. Survey averages for prime borrowers with about 20% down; individual offers vary with credit, points and lender. The cost of flexibility depends on the spread at the time of borrowing. Does not value the option itself (job loss, emergencies) and does not model investing the difference.
